passage: The terrace had a clothesline down the middle and only half an hour of light left. Sonali clapped for attention. "We don't have time to invent everything. Let's take from games we know." Parveen counted on her fingers. "Kabaddi has a home line and a chant. Tag has someone who is 'it'." "So a raider runs across and tries to touch someone," said Sonali, "and everyone else tries to tag the raider before they get back." The little ones were nodding. Within ten minutes, they were playing a game with kabaddi's line and tag's chasing, and nobody argued about what a rule meant.

passage: On the terrace of their Jaipur building, five children were bored of the same old games. "Let's invent a new one," Parul said. Vidya groaned. "We'll spend all evening making rules." Parul thought out loud. "What if we don't start from nothing? Kabaddi has two sides and a line in the middle. Tag has catching. So a raider crosses the line, tags someone and gets back, but instead of holding breath, the raider has to hop." Vidya's eyes lit up. "And if you're tagged, you join the other side, like in tag." They chalked a line down the middle of the terrace. Within ten minutes, the first raider was hopping across.

qa.q: What did they chalk on the terrace?
How did Vidya feel when Parul explained the idea?
qa.a: Vidya's eyes lit up, so Vidya went from bored and doubtful to excited about the game.

qa.q: What could the group do if their borrowed rules don't fit well?
qa.a: Play a round and change one rule at a time; borrowing from kabaddi and tag gave them a working start instead of a blank page.

qa.q: How might the other children on the terrace see the new game?
qa.a: They get a game that feels familiar yet new, so they can start playing within minutes instead of arguing over rules.

grounding: Shows children designing a terrace game by borrowing rules from kabaddi and tag, giving them a working start.

passage:
"I'm bored of kabaddi."
"I'm bored of tag."
"So let's make a new game," said Sangeeta.
"From scratch? That'll take forever," Anand said.
"Not scratch. Take bits. Kabaddi: two teams, a middle line, one raider goes over."
"And from tag?"
"The raider tags, and whoever's tagged has to freeze. Like freeze tag."
"How do they unfreeze?"
"A teammate crawls under their legs."
Anand counted the terrace tiles. "Middle line here. Teams of four."
"And the raider has to keep saying 'chaka-chak' instead of 'kabaddi'."
Everyone laughed. "Chaka-chak! Okay. First raid, Anand!"

qa.q: What does the raider have to keep saying?
How did Anand feel about making a new game at first?
qa.a: Anand felt doubtful and a bit impatient, thinking it would take forever from scratch.

qa.q: Which part of Sangeeta's thinking made the game quick to start?
qa.a: Taking pieces from games everyone already knew, kabaddi's teams and raider and tag's freezing, so nobody had to learn everything new.

qa.q: How do the others seem to feel about 'chaka-chak'?
qa.a: Everyone laughs, so they seem amused and excited to start.

grounding: Illustrates children building a new terrace game from pieces of kabaddi and tag, so they have a working start without inventing everything.
